column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: What is an allele?
column14: The trait you can see, like purple flowers
column15: One version of a gene, like the version for purple flowers or the version for white flowers
column16: A chart used to predict the offspring of a cross, like a cross between purple and white plants
column17: A sex cell, such as a sperm or an egg
column28: An allele is one form of a gene: the flower-color gene in peas has a purple allele and a white allele. The trait you can see is the phenotype, and the chart is a Punnett square. A common mistake is mixing up the allele (the version) with the phenotype (what shows).
column29: Think of a gene as a song and the alleles as different versions of that song.

column9: Which word names the pair of allele letters an organism has for a trait, such as Pp?
column28: The genotype is the letters (PP, Pp or pp). The phenotype is the trait you can see, such as purple flowers. Students often swap these two; remember genotype = genes = letters.
column29: One of these words starts the same way as the word gene.

column9: A tomato plant grows yellow fruit. What does "yellow fruit" describe?
column28: Yellow fruit is a trait you can see, so it is the phenotype. The genotype would be the allele letters, such as rr. A common mistake is calling any trait a genotype.
column29: Is yellow fruit something you can see, or a set of letters?

column9: Which genotype is heterozygous?
column28: Heterozygous means two different alleles, so Gg is heterozygous. GG and gg each have two of the same allele, so they are homozygous. A common mistake is thinking a capital letter alone makes something heterozygous.
column29: Hetero- means different.

column9: A fruit fly has the genotype ee. Which term describes this genotype?
column28: ee has two identical alleles (homozygous), and both are lowercase (recessive), so it is homozygous recessive. Heterozygous and hybrid both mean two different alleles, like Ee. A common mistake is calling any lowercase pair heterozygous.
column29: Are the two letters the same or different? Are they capital or lowercase?

column9: How is a dominant allele usually written in a genetics problem?
column14: As a capital letter, such as A
column15: As a lowercase letter, such as a
column17: As two lowercase letters, such as aa
column28: Dominant alleles get a capital letter and recessive alleles get the lowercase form of the same letter. A common mistake is using two different letters, like A and b, for the same gene.
column29: Think about which letter looks bigger and stronger.

column9: An allele whose trait is hidden whenever a dominant allele is present is called a(n) ___ allele.
column28: A recessive allele is hidden when a dominant allele is present, so its trait shows only with two copies. A common mistake is writing dominant, which is the allele that does the hiding.
column29: It "recedes," or steps back, when the dominant allele is around.

column9: An organism with two identical alleles for a trait, such as BB or bb, is called ___.
column28: Homozygous means two of the same allele, either both dominant (BB) or both recessive (bb). A common mistake is writing heterozygous, which means two different alleles (Bb).
column29: Homo- means same.

column9: A rabbit breeder's black rabbits have produced only black babies for many generations. Which word best describes these rabbits for fur color?
column28: Organisms that come from many generations with the same trait are purebred, which means homozygous. A hybrid (heterozygous) rabbit could sometimes have babies with a different fur color. Recessive describes an allele, not a whole rabbit.
column29: A rabbit that never has a different-colored baby probably carries only one kind of allele for fur color.

column9: A Punnett square for one trait between two parents has how many boxes?
column28: Each parent can pass on 2 possible alleles, so the square is 2 × 2 = 4 boxes. 16 boxes is the size for a cross that follows two traits at once. A common mistake is thinking each parent gets its own box.
column29: Each parent has 2 alleles to write on its edge of the square.

column9: What does each box inside a Punnett square stand for?
column14: The genotype of one of the parents, copied into each box from the top edge of the square
column15: The exact number of offspring the parents will have
column16: A single allele from just one parent, the same allele that will be passed on to every offspring
column17: One possible genotype an offspring could inherit, with the same chance as every other box
column28: Each box combines one allele from each parent, so it is one possible offspring genotype, and all four boxes are equally likely. The square shows chances, not an exact count of babies. A common mistake is thinking the boxes are the parents.
column29: Each box gets one letter from its column and one from its row. Whose genotype does that make?

column9: When you set up a Punnett square, what do you write across the top and down the side?
column14: Both parents' alleles across the top and the offspring's phenotypes down the side
column15: The possible offspring genotypes across the top and their matching phenotypes down the side of the square
column16: The alleles each parent can pass on: one parent's across the top and the other parent's down the side
column17: The grandparents' phenotypes across the top and the parents' phenotypes down the side, one generation per edge
column28: One parent's two alleles go across the top and the other parent's two alleles go down the side; the offspring are filled into the boxes. A common mistake is putting both parents on the same edge.
column29: The edges hold what goes INTO the offspring. The boxes hold the offspring.

column9: In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant over white flowers (p). What color are the flowers of a Pp plant?
column16: Light purple, a blend of the two colors
column17: Half purple and half white petals
column28: One dominant P is enough to make purple flowers, so Pp is purple. Blending and both-colors-showing happen in other inheritance patterns (incomplete dominance and codominance), not simple dominance. A common mistake is thinking a heterozygous plant shows a mix.
column29: With simple dominance, what happens when even one dominant allele is present?

column9: In house mice, black fur (B) is dominant over brown fur (b). Which genotype gives a brown mouse?
column28: Brown is recessive, so it shows only with two recessive alleles: bb. Bb has one B, which is enough for black fur. A common mistake is thinking Bb is brown because it has a b.
column29: A recessive trait needs two copies of the recessive allele.

column9: In cats, short hair (L) is dominant over long hair (l). Which genotypes give a short-haired cat? Select all that apply.
column28: LL and Ll both have at least one dominant L, so both cats have short hair. Only ll has long hair. A common mistake is choosing only LL and forgetting that heterozygous cats show the dominant trait too.
column29: How many copies of the dominant allele does it take to show the dominant trait?

column9: In cattle, being hornless (polled, P) is dominant over having horns (p). A PP bull is crossed with a pp cow. What genotype will every calf have?
column28: The bull can only give P and the cow can only give p, so every box is Pp, and all the calves are polled. A common mistake is thinking some calves will look just like each parent (PP or pp).
column29: What is the only allele each parent can pass on?

column9: Two pea plants that are both PP for flower color are crossed. Purple (P) is dominant over white (p). What percent of their offspring will have white flowers?
column28: Both parents can only pass on P, so every offspring is PP and purple: 0% white. A common mistake is assuming every cross gives some recessive offspring.
column29: Can either parent pass on a p allele?

column9: In corn, purple kernels (R) are dominant over yellow kernels (r). Two Rr corn plants are crossed. How many of the 4 boxes in the Punnett square show a yellow (rr) kernel? Enter just the number.
column28: The boxes are RR, Rr, Rr and rr. Only rr is yellow, so 1 box of 4. A common mistake is counting the Rr boxes as yellow; one R makes the kernel purple.
column29: Fill in the square with R and r on both edges, then look for boxes with two lowercase letters.

column9: In rabbits, normal fur (N) is dominant over long, fluffy angora fur (n). An Nn rabbit is crossed with an nn rabbit. Which genotypes can the babies have?
column28: The Nn parent gives N or n and the nn parent always gives n, so the boxes are Nn, Nn, nn, nn. NN is impossible because only one parent has an N to give. A common mistake is listing NN, which needs an N from both parents.
column29: Write N and n across the top and n and n down the side.

column9: What is a phenotype?
column14: The pair of alleles an organism carries for a gene
column15: A single allele carried in a sperm or egg
column16: The trait that actually shows, such as fur color or flower color
column17: A list of all the genes in an organism
column28: A phenotype is the observable trait, like brown fur. The pair of alleles is the genotype. A common mistake is reversing the two words.
column29: Pheno- is related to a Greek word meaning to show.

column9: Match each genetics term to its meaning.
column14: Allele :: One version of a gene
column15: Genotype :: The allele letters an organism has, like Tt
column16: Phenotype :: The trait you can see, like tall
column28: An allele is one version of a gene, the genotype is the letters, the phenotype is what you see, homozygous is two of the same, and heterozygous is two different. The most common mix-up is genotype and phenotype.
column29: Homo- means same and hetero- means different. Genotype goes with genes (letters).

column9: How many alleles for a single gene does a normal body cell carry?
column28: A body cell has two alleles for each gene, one inherited from each parent. That is why genotypes are written with two letters. A common mistake is thinking each cell has only the allele that shows.
column29: Why is every genotype written with two letters?

column9: In a genetics problem written as Tt × tt, what does the × mean?
column14: Multiply the number of alleles together
column15: The offspring will be Tt and tt
column16: The trait is carried on the X chromosome
column17: The two parents are being crossed (mated)
column28: In genetics, × means a cross between the two parents listed. The offspring are found by filling in the Punnett square, not by reading the parents' genotypes. A common mistake is treating the × as math or as the X chromosome.
column29: The two genotypes on each side of the × belong to the parents.

column9: In a Punnett square for one trait, each of the 4 boxes stands for a ___% chance.
column28: The 4 boxes are equally likely and share 100%, so each box is 100 ÷ 4 = 25%. A common mistake is saying 50% because there are two parents.
column29: Split 100% into 4 equal parts.

column9: In summer squash, white fruit (W) is dominant over yellow fruit (w). A Punnett square shows these four boxes: Ww, Ww, ww, ww. What is the genotypic ratio?
column28: Count the boxes: 2 Ww and 2 ww, so 2:2, which simplifies to 1:1. 1:2:1 is the genotypic ratio for two heterozygous parents. A common mistake is using a memorized ratio instead of counting the boxes.
column29: Count how many boxes have each genotype.

column9: In pea plants, green pods (G) are dominant over yellow pods (g). A Punnett square shows GG, GG, Gg and Gg. What is the phenotypic ratio?
column28: Every box has at least one G, so all 4 offspring have green pods. 1 GG : 1 Gg is the genotypic ratio, not the phenotypic one. A common mistake is counting Gg as yellow.
column29: Phenotype means what the pod looks like. Which boxes have at least one G?

column9: Which of these is a genotype rather than a phenotype?
column28: Ss is a pair of allele letters, so it is a genotype. The others are traits you can see, which are phenotypes. A common mistake is thinking any trait name is a genotype.
column29: Genotypes are written in letters.

column9: In simple dominant–recessive inheritance, a recessive trait shows up only when an organism has two copies of the recessive allele.
column28: True. A recessive trait is hidden by a dominant allele, so it shows only in the homozygous recessive genotype, like aa. A common mistake is thinking Aa shows the recessive trait.
column29: What happens to a recessive allele when a dominant allele is also present?

column9: Two pea plants that are both tall must have the same genotype for height.
column28: False. If tall (T) is dominant, a tall plant could be TT or Tt, so two tall plants can have different genotypes. A common mistake is thinking the same look always means the same letters.
column29: How many different genotypes show the dominant trait?

column9: In a Punnett square, 3 of the 4 boxes show offspring with the dominant phenotype. What percent of the offspring are expected to show the dominant phenotype? Enter just the number, without the % sign.
column28: Each box is 25%, so 3 boxes × 25% = 75%. A common mistake is entering 3 (the number of boxes) instead of the percent.
column29: Each box is worth the same percent. How much is one box worth?

column9: In horses, a black-based coat (E) is dominant over a chestnut (reddish) coat (e). Two chestnut horses (ee × ee) are bred. What will their foals be?
column28: Both parents can only pass on e, so every foal is ee and chestnut. A common mistake is expecting a dominant trait to appear when neither parent has the dominant allele.
column29: Does either parent have an E to pass on?

column9: Which statement about a dominant allele is true?
column14: It is always the most common allele in a population
column15: It is always better for the organism's survival
column16: Its trait shows even when only one copy is present
column17: It needs two copies before its trait shows
column28: Dominant only means the trait shows with one copy. It does not mean the allele is common or helpful. A common mistake is thinking dominant means stronger or more common.
column29: Dominant describes what happens inside one organism with one copy of the allele.

column9: In humans, normal skin pigment (A) is dominant over albinism (a). What is true about a person with the genotype Aa?
column15: They have normal pigment but carry the albinism allele
column16: They have a mild, in-between form of albinism
column17: They do not carry the albinism allele at all
column28: The dominant A gives normal pigment, but the person still carries one a allele and can pass it to children. A person like this is called a carrier. A common mistake is thinking the hidden allele disappears.
column29: The dominant allele decides what shows, but both alleles are still there.

column9: In sheep, white wool (W) is dominant over black wool (w). What is the genotype of a black sheep?
column17: You can't tell from its wool color
column28: Black is recessive, so a black sheep must be ww. The dominant phenotype (white) is the one where you can't be sure of the genotype. A common mistake is thinking you can never tell a genotype by looking.
column29: Which phenotype has only one possible genotype?

column9: In tomatoes, red fruit (R) is dominant over yellow fruit (r). An RR plant is crossed with an Rr plant. What percent of the offspring will have red fruit?
column28: The boxes are RR, RR, Rr and Rr. Every box has an R, so 100% have red fruit. A common mistake is answering 50% because only half are RR; Rr plants are red too.
column29: Phenotype is about color. How many boxes have at least one R?

column9: Put the steps for solving a Punnett square problem in order.
column14: Count the boxes to find the genotypic ratio
column16: Use the dominant and recessive alleles to find the phenotypic ratio
column17: Write one parent's alleles across the top and the other's down the side
column18: Fill each box with one allele from its column and one from its row
column28: First write the parents' genotypes, then put their alleles on the edges, fill in the boxes, count genotypes, and finally decide what each genotype looks like. A common mistake is finding the phenotypes before the boxes are filled in.
column29: You need the parents before the edges, and the boxes before any ratio.

column9: A monohybrid cross follows how many traits at once?
column28: Mono- means one, so a monohybrid cross follows one trait, like flower color. A cross that follows two traits at once is a dihybrid cross. A common mistake is thinking mono- refers to one parent.
column29: Think of other words that start with mono-, like monorail.

column9: In a species of beetle, green shells (G) are dominant over brown shells (g). A beetle with the genotype gg has ___ shells.
column28: gg has two recessive alleles and no G, so the recessive trait shows: brown. A common mistake is choosing green because green is dominant, but there is no dominant allele here.
column29: Is there a capital G anywhere in this genotype?

column9: In fruit flies, normal wings (V) are dominant over shriveled, vestigial wings (v). The Punnett square for Vv × Vv has the boxes VV, Vv, Vv and vv. How many of the 4 boxes are heterozygous? Enter just the number.
column28: Heterozygous means two different alleles. Vv appears in 2 boxes. A common mistake is entering 3, which is the number of boxes with normal wings, not the number that are heterozygous.
column29: Look for boxes with one capital and one lowercase letter.

column9: Which pair of parents can produce ONLY heterozygous offspring?
column28: AA can only give A and aa can only give a, so every offspring is Aa. Each of the other crosses has a parent that can give either allele, which makes some homozygous offspring. A common mistake is choosing Aa × Aa because both parents are heterozygous.
column29: Find the cross where each parent can pass on only one kind of allele, and the two kinds are different.

column9: Which word is another name for a heterozygous organism, such as a Tt plant?
column28: A hybrid has two different alleles for a trait, which is the same as heterozygous. Purebred means homozygous. A common mistake is mixing up hybrid and purebred.
column29: A hybrid car mixes two kinds of power. A hybrid organism mixes two kinds of...?

column9: A pea plant is Rr for seed shape. Which alleles can it pass on in a single pollen grain or egg?
column14: Either R or r, but only one of them
column15: Only R, because it is dominant
column16: Only r, because it is recessive
column28: Each sex cell gets just one allele of each pair, so a pollen grain or egg from an Rr plant has either R or r. That is why the two letters are split up on the edge of the Punnett square. A common mistake is thinking only the dominant allele gets passed on.
column29: Why do you write a parent's two letters separately on the edge of the square?

column9: A Punnett square gives a phenotypic ratio of 1:1. What percent of the offspring are expected to show each phenotype?
column28: 1:1 means equal parts, so each phenotype is 2 of 4 boxes, or 50%. A common mistake is thinking 1:1 means 1 box, or 25%.
column29: If the two phenotypes are equal, how do they split 100%?

column9: In dogs, a black coat (B) is dominant over a brown coat (b) for one gene. A breeder describes a dog as homozygous dominant for coat color. Which genotype is that?
column28: Homozygous means two of the same allele, and dominant means capital letters, so BB. Bb is heterozygous and bb is homozygous recessive. A common mistake is choosing Bb because it shows the dominant trait.
column29: Homozygous means same. Dominant means capital.

column9: Two Dd parents are crossed. Which set of boxes is the correct completed Punnett square?
column28: With D and d on both edges, the boxes are D+D = DD, D+d = Dd, d+D = Dd, and d+d = dd. A common mistake is copying a parent's genotype into each box (all Dd) instead of combining one letter from each edge.
column29: Write D and d across the top and down the side, then combine the letters for each box.

column9: In Labrador retrievers (looking at just one gene), black coat (B) is dominant over chocolate coat (b). A heterozygous black Lab is crossed with a chocolate Lab. What percent of the puppies are expected to be chocolate?
column28: Bb × bb gives the boxes Bb, Bb, bb, bb. The 2 bb boxes are chocolate: 2 of 4 = 50%. A common mistake is answering 25%, which is the answer when both parents are heterozygous.
column29: First turn the words into genotypes: heterozygous black and chocolate.

column9: In pea plants, flowers along the stem (axial, A) are dominant over flowers only at the tip (terminal, a). Two Aa plants are crossed, and 200 of their seeds grow into plants. About how many plants are expected to have terminal flowers? Enter just the number.
column28: Aa × Aa gives 1 aa box of 4, so 1/4 are terminal. 1/4 of 200 = 50. A common mistake is entering 150, which is the number expected to have axial (dominant) flowers.
column29: Find the fraction that is aa, then take that fraction of 200.

column9: In chickens, a rose comb (R) is dominant over a single comb (r). Two Rr chickens are crossed. What is the expected phenotypic ratio of their chicks?
column28: Rr × Rr gives RR, Rr, Rr, rr. RR and Rr both have rose combs, so 3 rose : 1 single. A common mistake is giving the genotypic ratio (1:2:1) when the question asks about phenotypes.
column29: After you fill in the square, group the boxes by what the comb looks like.

column9: In pea plants, yellow seeds (Y) are dominant over green seeds (y). Two Yy plants are crossed. What percent of the offspring are expected to be homozygous (either YY or yy)?
column28: The boxes are YY, Yy, Yy, yy. Homozygous boxes are YY and yy: 2 of 4 = 50%. A common mistake is counting only YY (25%) and forgetting that homozygous recessive is homozygous too.
column29: Homozygous includes both kinds of matching pairs.

column9: In cattle, polled (hornless, P) is dominant over horned (p). A PP bull is crossed with several Pp cows, and 20 calves are born. How many of the calves are expected to have horns? Enter just the number.
column28: The bull always gives P, so every calf is PP or Pp, and all are polled. 0 horned calves are expected. A common mistake is assuming a heterozygous parent always produces some recessive offspring; that needs a recessive allele from BOTH parents.
column29: To have horns a calf needs pp. Can the bull give a p?

column9: A Punnett square has the four boxes KK, KK, Kk and Kk. What were the parents' genotypes?
column28: Every box has a K from one parent, so that parent must be KK. The other parent gave K to two boxes and k to two boxes, so it is Kk. A common mistake is choosing Kk × Kk, which would also make a kk box.
column29: One parent gave the same letter to every box. What did the other parent give?

column9: A student filled in a Punnett square for Aa × aa and got AA, Aa, Aa and aa. What mistake did the student make?
column14: They forgot to write the dominant allele first in each box
column15: They should have used 8 boxes instead of 4
column16: They set it up as Aa × Aa instead of Aa × aa
column17: There is no mistake; Aa × aa gives these boxes
column28: The aa parent can only give a, so no box can be AA. The student's boxes are what Aa × Aa makes, so they wrote A and a on both edges. The correct boxes are Aa, Aa, aa, aa. A common mistake is not checking each edge against the parent's genotype.
column29: Which parent could give an A? Could any box get two A's?

column9: In tomato plants, tall vines (D) are dominant over dwarf vines (d). A Dd plant is crossed with a dd plant. What is the expected phenotypic ratio of tall to dwarf? Type it like 3:1. ___
column28: Dd × dd gives Dd, Dd, dd, dd: 2 tall and 2 dwarf, so 2:2, which simplifies to 1:1. A common mistake is answering 3:1, which only comes from two heterozygous parents.
column29: Fill in the square, then count tall boxes and dwarf boxes.

column9: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is caused by a recessive allele (f). Two parents are both carriers (Ff). What is the chance that their child will have CF?
column28: Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff. Only ff has CF: 1 of 4 = 25%. A common mistake is answering 50% by counting the carrier boxes (Ff) as having the disease.
column29: Which genotype actually has the recessive disorder?

column9: A person with cystic fibrosis (ff) has children with a person who is homozygous for the normal allele (FF). What is the chance that each child has CF? (CF is recessive.)
column28: Every child gets f from one parent and F from the other, so all children are Ff. They are carriers but do not have CF: 0%. A common mistake is thinking a parent with the disorder must pass the disorder itself on.
column29: Every child gets one allele from each parent. What does the FF parent always give?

column9: In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant over white flowers (p). Which crosses could produce at least one white-flowered offspring? Select all that apply.
column28: A white offspring (pp) needs a p from each parent. Pp × Pp, Pp × pp and pp × pp all have both parents able to give p. Any cross with a PP parent always gives a P, so it can't make white offspring. A common mistake is thinking PP × pp makes some white plants.
column29: For a pp offspring, BOTH parents must be able to pass on a p.

column9: In house mice, black fur (B) is dominant over brown fur (b). Two Bb mice have 12 babies over several litters. About how many babies are expected to be brown? Enter just the number.
column28: Bb × Bb gives 1 bb box of 4, so 1/4 of the babies are expected to be brown. 1/4 of 12 = 3. A common mistake is entering 6 by treating the cross as a 1:1 ratio.
column29: What fraction of the Punnett square is bb?

column9: What is a test cross used for?
column14: To find out whether an organism with the dominant trait is homozygous or heterozygous
column15: To find out which allele is dominant by crossing two recessive organisms
column16: To make sure every offspring has the dominant trait
column17: To count the chromosomes in an organism's cells
column28: An organism with the dominant phenotype could be AA or Aa. A test cross reveals which one from the offspring it produces. A common mistake is thinking a test cross is any experiment that tests a trait.
column29: Which organisms have a genotype you can't figure out just by looking?

column9: In a test cross, the organism showing the dominant trait is crossed with an organism that is:
column16: Any organism of the same species
column28: The partner in a test cross is homozygous recessive (aa) because it can only pass on recessive alleles, so any recessive offspring must have gotten a recessive allele from the unknown parent. A common mistake is choosing homozygous dominant, which would hide the unknown parent's alleles.
column29: Pick the partner that would let the unknown parent's alleles show up in the offspring.

column9: In pea plants, inflated pods (I) are dominant over constricted (pinched) pods (i). Two Ii plants are crossed. What fraction of the offspring are expected to have inflated pods?
column28: Ii × Ii gives II, Ii, Ii, ii. Three boxes have an I, so 3/4 have inflated pods. A common mistake is answering 1/4 by counting only II.
column29: Inflated is the dominant trait. How many boxes have at least one I?

column9: Match each cross to its expected genotypic ratio.
column28: AA × aa makes only Aa; Aa × Aa makes all three genotypes in 1:2:1; Aa × aa makes half Aa and half aa; AA × Aa makes half AA and half Aa. A common mistake is mixing up Aa × aa and AA × Aa, which both have one heterozygous parent.
column29: Sketch a quick Punnett square for each cross.

column9: Put these crosses in order from the LOWEST to the HIGHEST percent of offspring expected to show the dominant phenotype.
column28: aa × aa gives 0% dominant, Aa × aa gives 50%, Aa × Aa gives 75%, and AA × aa gives 100%. A common mistake is ranking Aa × Aa last because both parents are heterozygous, but AA × aa gives every offspring an A.
column29: Work out the percent with at least one A for each cross, then sort.

column9: A Punnett square for two tall parent plants predicts that 1 out of every 4 of their offspring will be short. A gardener grows only 4 plants from this cross, and none of them are short. What is the best explanation?
column14: The Punnett square must be wrong, so the parents must both be homozygous tall and can't have short offspring
column15: Short plants can't grow from tall parents
column16: The short allele must have changed into the tall allele
column17: Each seed is a separate chance event, and small samples often don't match the predicted ratio
column28: A Punnett square gives probabilities, not guarantees. With only 4 plants, getting 0 short is quite possible by chance. With hundreds of plants, the results would get close to 1 in 4. A common mistake is thinking the ratio must come out exactly in every small family.
column29: Think about flipping a coin 4 times. Do you always get exactly 2 heads?

column9: In corn, purple kernels (R) are dominant over yellow kernels (r). An ear of corn from an Rr × Rr cross has 400 kernels. About how many kernels are expected to be purple? Enter just the number.
column28: Rr × Rr gives 3 purple boxes of 4, so 3/4 of 400 = 300 purple kernels. A common mistake is entering 100, which is the expected number of yellow kernels.
column29: What fraction of the boxes have at least one R?

column9: Huntington's disease is caused by a dominant allele (H). A parent who is Hh has children with a parent who is hh. What is the chance that each child inherits Huntington's disease?
column28: Hh × hh gives Hh, Hh, hh, hh. Because the disease allele is dominant, the 2 Hh boxes have the disease: 50%. A common mistake is treating the disease as recessive and answering 25% or 0%.
column29: In this disorder, which allele causes the disease: the capital or the lowercase one?

column9: A cross gives a 3:1 phenotypic ratio of dominant to recessive offspring. What must be true about the parents?
column15: One is homozygous dominant and one is homozygous recessive
column16: One is heterozygous and one is homozygous recessive
column28: Only a cross of two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) gives one recessive box out of four. AA × aa gives all dominant, Aa × aa gives 1:1, and AA × AA gives all dominant. A common mistake is choosing heterozygous × recessive, which gives 1:1.
column29: For 1 recessive box in 4, both parents must be able to give a recessive allele, but not every time.

column9: When two heterozygous parents are crossed, the genotypic ratio has three parts but the phenotypic ratio has only two. Why?
column14: Heterozygous offspring show a blend of the two traits
column15: The homozygous recessive offspring do not survive, so their group drops out of the phenotype count
column16: A Punnett square counts only the dominant alleles
column17: AA and Aa offspring look the same, because one dominant allele is enough to show the trait
column28: AA and Aa are different genotypes but the same phenotype, so they join into one phenotype group. That leaves 2 phenotypes from 3 genotypes. A common mistake is thinking heterozygous offspring blend, which is incomplete dominance, a different pattern.
column29: Which two genotypes look exactly alike?

column9: A heterozygous purple-flowered pea plant (Pp) pollinates itself. What is the chance that one of its seeds grows into a white-flowered plant?
column28: Pollinating itself means the cross is Pp × Pp, which gives 1 pp box in 4, so 25% white. A common mistake is thinking self-pollination can only make copies of the parent.
column29: Self-pollinating means the plant is both parents. Write Pp on both edges.

column9: A student says, "Purple is dominant, so a Pp × pp cross will give mostly purple offspring." Is the student right?
column14: Yes; a dominant trait always shows up in most of the offspring
column15: No; the cross is expected to give half purple and half white offspring
column16: Yes; about 75% of the offspring will be purple
column17: No; all of the offspring will be white
column28: Pp × pp gives Pp, Pp, pp, pp: 50% purple and 50% white. Dominant means the trait shows with one copy, not that it shows up in most offspring. A common mistake is assuming dominant traits always win the ratio.
column29: Fill in the square instead of trusting the word dominant.

column9: In cats, short hair (L) is dominant over long hair (l). Two Ll cats are crossed. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
column14: About 1 in 4 kittens is expected to have long hair
column15: About half of the kittens are expected to be heterozygous
column16: All of the kittens will have short hair
column17: About 3 in 4 kittens are expected to have short hair
column18: None of the kittens can be homozygous
column28: Ll × Ll gives LL, Ll, Ll, ll. So 1/4 are long-haired (ll), 2/4 are heterozygous (Ll), and 3/4 are short-haired. LL and ll are both homozygous, so homozygous kittens are possible. A common mistake is thinking heterozygous parents can't have a long-haired kitten.
column29: Fill in the square first, then test each statement against the four boxes.

column9: Two hamsters that are both heterozygous (Gg) for coat color have 16 pups over several litters. About how many of the pups are expected to be heterozygous (Gg)? Enter just the number.
column28: Gg × Gg gives GG, Gg, Gg, gg. 2 of 4 boxes are Gg, so half of 16 = 8. A common mistake is entering 12, which counts every pup with the dominant phenotype instead of only the heterozygous ones.
column29: Count only the boxes with two different letters.

column9: Mendel crossed purebred purple-flowered pea plants with purebred white-flowered pea plants. Every offspring had purple flowers. What does this tell you?
column15: The white allele was destroyed in the offspring
column28: The offspring got one purple and one white allele, and they all looked purple, so purple is dominant. The white allele was hidden, not destroyed; it can show up again in later generations. A common mistake is thinking the hidden allele is gone.
column29: Each offspring had one allele of each kind. Which one showed?

column9: A cross produces offspring that ALL show the recessive phenotype. What must the parents' genotypes be?
column16: One heterozygous and one homozygous recessive
column17: One homozygous dominant and one homozygous recessive
column28: If every offspring is aa, every parent must only be able to give a, so both parents are aa. Any parent with an A could pass it on and make dominant offspring. A common mistake is choosing heterozygous × recessive, which gives only half recessive.
column29: What allele must every offspring get from each parent?

column9: Two Nn parents are crossed. What fraction of the offspring are expected to be NN? Type a fraction like 1/2. ___
column28: Nn × Nn gives NN, Nn, Nn, nn. Only 1 box of 4 is NN, so 1/4. A common mistake is answering 3/4, which is the fraction showing the dominant phenotype, not the fraction that is NN.
column29: Count only the boxes with two capital letters.

column9: Which offspring genotype is impossible from the cross DD × Dd?
column28: The DD parent always gives D, so every offspring has at least one D. dd would need a d from both parents, so it can't happen. A common mistake is thinking any cross with a heterozygous parent can make a recessive offspring.
column29: Can the DD parent ever give a d?

column9: A seed company sells "tall" pea seeds. Customers report that about 1 out of every 4 plants they grow is short. Tall (T) is dominant over short (t). What does this suggest about the parent plants used to make the seeds?
column15: One parent was TT and the other was tt
column16: Both parents were heterozygous (Tt), not purebred tall
column17: The short plants came from poor soil, since tall × tall can never give short
column28: A 3 tall : 1 short ratio comes from Tt × Tt. TT × TT and TT × tt would give 0% short. A common mistake is thinking tall parents can never have short offspring, but heterozygous parents can each pass on t.
column29: Which cross gives 1 short box out of 4?

column9: A researcher crosses a fruit fly with normal wings with a fly that has vestigial wings (normal V is dominant over vestigial v). The offspring are 52 flies with normal wings and 48 with vestigial wings. What were the parents' genotypes?
column28: 52:48 is very close to 1:1, and Vv × vv gives 2 Vv : 2 vv. VV × vv would give no vestigial flies, and Vv × Vv would give about 3:1. A common mistake is expecting the data to match the ratio exactly instead of looking for the closest ratio.
column29: Which simple ratio is 52:48 closest to? Which cross gives that ratio?

column9: A rancher does a test cross: she breeds her polled (hornless) bull with several horned cows. Polled (P) is dominant over horned (p). All 12 calves are polled. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: The bull is most likely PP
column16: The bull is most likely pp
column17: The horned cows must have been Pp
column28: If the bull were Pp, about half of the calves would be horned. Getting 12 polled calves in a row would be very unlikely, so the bull is most likely PP. It can't be pp because he is polled, and horned cows must be pp. A common mistake is saying definitely, since chance can never be ruled out completely.
column29: If the bull carried a p, what fraction of calves would you expect to have horns?

column9: A breeder wants to know whether her black Labrador (black B is dominant over chocolate b) carries the chocolate allele. Which plan is best?
column14: Breed her with a BB black dog and look for any chocolate puppies
column15: Look at her coat under bright light for brown patches
column16: Breed her with a black dog once and check whether the first puppy is black
column17: Breed her with a chocolate (bb) dog and look for any chocolate puppies
column28: This is a test cross. A bb partner always gives b, so if she is Bb, about half of the puppies will be chocolate. A BB partner always gives B, which would hide her b, and one puppy is too little evidence. A common mistake is choosing a dominant partner, which can't reveal a hidden allele.
column29: Pick the partner that would let a hidden b from the black dog show up in a puppy.

column9: A Punnett square for two parents shows the boxes Ss, Ss, ss and ss. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
column16: 50% of the offspring are expected to show the recessive trait
column17: Both parents show the dominant trait
column18: 75% of the offspring are expected to show the dominant trait
column28: One parent gave S to two boxes and s to two boxes (Ss), and the other gave s to every box (ss). Half the boxes are ss, so 50% recessive and 50% dominant. The ss parent shows the recessive trait. A common mistake is assuming both parents look alike.
column29: Work backward from the boxes: what did each parent give to every box?

column9: In pea plants, round seeds (R) are dominant over wrinkled seeds (r). Purebred round plants are crossed with purebred wrinkled plants. Then their offspring are crossed with each other. What fraction of the plants in this second generation are expected to have wrinkled seeds?
column28: RR × rr gives all Rr offspring. Then Rr × Rr gives RR, Rr, Rr, rr, so 1/4 are wrinkled. A common mistake is stopping after the first cross and answering 0.
column29: Do it in two steps: first find the offspring's genotype, then cross two of them.

column9: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a recessive disorder (k). Two parents are both carriers (Kk). Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
column14: Each child has a 1 in 4 chance of having PKU
column15: If their first child has PKU, their second child still has a 1 in 4 chance of having PKU
column16: Exactly one out of every four children they have will have PKU
column17: Each child has a 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier (Kk)
column18: A child without PKU cannot be a carrier
column28: Kk × Kk gives KK, Kk, Kk, kk: a 1/4 chance of PKU and a 1/2 chance of being a carrier for every child. Each child is a new chance event, so earlier children don't change the odds and the 1-in-4 is not a guarantee. Children without PKU can be Kk carriers. A common mistake is treating the ratio as an exact count.
column29: The Punnett square resets for every child, like a new coin flip.

column9: Two parents with normal skin pigment have a child with albinism (aa). Normal pigment (A) is dominant. What is the chance that their next child will have normal pigment?
column28: The aa child got an a from each parent, and both parents have normal pigment, so both are Aa. Aa × Aa gives 3 boxes of 4 with an A, so 75% normal pigment. A common mistake is answering 25%, which is the chance of albinism, not of normal pigment.
column29: First use the child to find the parents' genotypes. Then make the square.

column9: In rabbits, black fur (B) is dominant over white fur (b). Two Bb rabbits have 40 babies over several litters. About how many babies are expected to be black AND heterozygous? Enter just the number.
column28: Bb × Bb gives BB, Bb, Bb, bb. The black and heterozygous babies are the Bb boxes: 2 of 4 = 1/2, and 1/2 of 40 = 20. A common mistake is entering 30, which counts all black babies, including the BB ones.
column29: Not every black baby is heterozygous. Which boxes are both black and Bb?

column9: In house mice, black fur (B) is dominant over brown fur (b). A Bb mouse and a bb mouse have 18 brown babies. If the results matched the expected ratio exactly, how many babies were born in total? Enter just the number.
column28: Bb × bb gives half brown (bb). If 18 babies are half of the total, the total is 18 × 2 = 36. A common mistake is entering 72 by using a 1/4 fraction, which is for two heterozygous parents.
column29: What fraction of the babies from this cross are brown? Then work backward from 18.

column9: From a cross of two heterozygous plants, 90 of the offspring showed the dominant trait. If the results matched the expected ratio, about how many offspring showed the recessive trait? Enter just the number.
column28: Two heterozygous parents give 3 dominant : 1 recessive. 90 dominant is 3 parts, so 1 part is 90 ÷ 3 = 30 recessive. A common mistake is entering 90 ÷ 4 = 22.5 or 22, which treats 90 as the total.
column29: 90 is not the total. It is the dominant part of the ratio.

column9: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over short (t). A TT plant is crossed with a Tt plant. One of their tall offspring is picked at random and crossed with a short (tt) plant. What is the chance that this second cross can produce any short offspring?
column28: TT × Tt gives TT, TT, Tt, Tt, so half the offspring are Tt. Only a Tt plant can give a t to make short plants, so the chance is 1/2. A common mistake is answering 0 because all the offspring are tall, but tall plants can still carry t.
column29: First find the genotypes from TT × Tt. What fraction of them hide a t?

column9: In house mice, black fur (B) is dominant over brown fur (b). Two black mice have a brown baby. When that brown baby grows up and mates with a BB black mouse, what genotype will ALL of its babies have? ___
column28: The brown baby must be bb. Crossing bb × BB gives a b and a B to every baby, so all are Bb. A common mistake is writing BB, forgetting that the brown parent can only give b.
column29: Start with the brown baby's genotype, then make the new square.

column9: A farmer wants EVERY lamb to have white wool, and she can choose only from these pairs of sheep. White wool (W) is dominant over black wool (w). Which pair should she choose?
column28: WW always gives W, so every lamb gets at least one W and is white. Ww × Ww would give about 1/4 black lambs, Ww × ww about 1/2, and ww × ww all black. A common mistake is choosing Ww × Ww because both parents are white.
column29: Look for a pair where every lamb is guaranteed to get a W.

column9: Polydactyly (having extra fingers or toes) can be caused by a dominant allele, yet it is rare. A student says, "That can't be right. Dominant traits are always the most common." Which response is best?
column14: Dominant means the trait shows when one copy is present; it says nothing about how many people carry the allele
column15: The student is right, so polydactyly must actually be recessive
column16: Dominant traits only become common in plants, not in people
column17: Polydactyly is rare because dominant alleles are destroyed when sperm and eggs form
column28: Dominance describes what happens in one person's genotype. How common a trait is depends on how many people carry the allele. Few people carry the polydactyly allele, so it is rare even though it is dominant. A common mistake is confusing dominant with common.
column29: Does dominant describe what happens inside one person, or how many people have the allele?

column9: A cross produces offspring in a 1 AA : 1 Aa genotypic ratio. Which statement about these offspring is true?
column14: Half of the offspring show the recessive phenotype
column16: One parent must have been aa
column17: Every offspring shows the dominant phenotype
column28: AA and Aa both have an A, so all of the offspring show the dominant phenotype. This ratio comes from AA × Aa. Two heterozygous parents would also make aa, and an aa parent couldn't make AA offspring. A common mistake is reading 1:1 as half dominant and half recessive.
column29: Look at each genotype in the ratio and decide what it looks like.

column9: A student solving Gg × gg writes "Gg" as one heading across the top and "gg" as one heading down the side, then fills the box with four letters: "Gggg." What is the mistake?
column14: The student should have written phenotypes on the edges instead, such as green across the top and yellow down
column15: The dominant allele should be written last in the box
column16: Each edge should list single alleles (G and g across, g and g down), so each box gets just two letters
column17: There is no mistake; this is the correct method, because each parent's whole genotype goes on one edge
column28: Each sex cell carries one allele, so each parent's two alleles are split onto separate rows or columns. That makes 4 boxes with two letters each: Gg, Gg, gg, gg. A common mistake is writing whole genotypes on the edges.
column29: How many alleles does each sperm or egg carry?

column9: For the cross Aa × Aa, put these outcomes in order from MOST likely to LEAST likely for one offspring (or, for the last one, for two offspring).
column15: The offspring shows the dominant phenotype
column17: Two offspring in a row are both homozygous recessive (aa)
column28: Dominant phenotype is 3/4, heterozygous is 1/2, aa is 1/4, and two aa in a row is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. A common mistake is ranking heterozygous above dominant phenotype, but the dominant group includes both AA and Aa.
column29: Write each as a fraction. For two offspring in a row, multiply the chances.

column9: Put these crosses in order from FEWEST to MOST different offspring genotypes possible.
column28: AA × AA makes only AA (1 genotype), Aa × aa makes Aa and aa (2), and Aa × Aa makes AA, Aa and aa (3). A common mistake is counting boxes (always 4) instead of different genotypes.
column29: Sketch each square and list the different genotypes, not the number of boxes.

column9: A purple pea plant is crossed with a white pea plant (purple P is dominant over white p), and half of the offspring are purple. If one of those purple offspring pollinates itself, what fraction of ITS offspring are expected to be white?
column28: Half purple means the cross was Pp × pp, so each purple offspring is Pp. Pp pollinating itself is Pp × Pp, which gives 1/4 white. A common mistake is answering 0 by assuming the purple offspring are PP.
column29: First figure out the purple offspring's genotype from the 1:1 result.

column9: A student crosses two Tt pea plants and grows 400 plants: 294 tall and 106 short. She says, "My results prove the Punnett square is wrong, because I didn't get exactly 300 tall and 100 short." Which response is best?
column14: She is right; any difference from 300:100 means the parents weren't Tt
column15: The results show that the parents were actually Tt × tt
column16: 294:106 is close to 3:1; real results vary by chance, so the data support the prediction
column17: She should have expected 200 tall and 200 short
column28: 294 ÷ 106 is about 2.8, which is close to 3. Chance makes real results a little off, but the data fit Tt × Tt. Tt × tt would give about 200:200. A common mistake is thinking a prediction is only right if it matches exactly.
column29: Divide tall by short. Is the answer near 3?

column9: Mendel crossed heterozygous round-seeded pea plants and counted 5,474 round seeds and 1,850 wrinkled seeds. Divide the number of round seeds by the number of wrinkled seeds. What is the ratio, to the nearest tenth? (Enter just the number, for example 2.5 for 2.5:1.)
column28: 5,474 ÷ 1,850 ≈ 2.96, which rounds to 3.0, so Mendel's data were about 3 round : 1 wrinkled, just as the Punnett square for Rr × Rr predicts. A common mistake is dividing wrinkled by round (about 0.34).
column29: Put round seeds on top when you divide.

column9: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is recessive (f). A man who does not have CF, but whose mother had CF, has children with a woman who has CF. What is the chance that each child will have CF?
column28: The man's mother was ff, so she gave him an f; he doesn't have CF, so he is Ff. The woman is ff. Ff × ff gives Ff, Ff, ff, ff, so 50% have CF. A common mistake is assuming the man is FF because he doesn't have the disorder.
column29: Use his mother to figure out the man's genotype first.

column9: For the cross Pp × pp, one student says the genotypic ratio is 1:1. Another says the phenotypic ratio is 1:1. Who is right?
column28: The boxes are Pp, Pp, pp, pp. Genotypes: 2 Pp : 2 pp = 1:1. Phenotypes: 2 dominant : 2 recessive = 1:1. Here each genotype has its own phenotype, so the ratios match. A common mistake is assuming the two ratios are always different.
column29: Fill in the square, then find both ratios separately.

column9: A Punnett square predicts that 100% of the offspring will show the dominant trait. Which pair of parents could NOT have been used?
column28: Aa × Aa predicts 1 aa box of 4, so 25% would show the recessive trait. Every other pair has an AA parent, so every offspring gets at least one A. A common mistake is thinking two parents with the dominant trait always have offspring with the dominant trait.
column29: Look for the pair where both parents could pass on an a.
